## Solution

The answer is **no** — under the stated hypotheses, a continuous selection need not exist. A counterexample suffices.

### Counterexample

Take $n = 1$. Then $\mathbf{R}^n = \mathbf{R}$, $\mathbf{S}^{n-1} = \mathbf{S}^0 = \{-1, +1\}$ (a two-point discrete space). Let

$$A = [0,\,1] \subseteq \mathbf{R},$$

which is closed. Define the fibers

$$
B_a = \begin{cases}
\{+1\}, & a \in [0,\tfrac12),\\[4pt]
\{-1,+1\}, & a = \tfrac12,\\[4pt]
\{-1\}, & a \in (\tfrac12,1].
\end{cases}
$$

Each $B_a$ is a finite (hence closed) subset of $\mathbf{S}^0$. The corresponding bundle is

$$B \;=\; \bigl([0,\tfrac12]\times\{+1\}\bigr)\;\cup\;\bigl([\tfrac12,1]\times\{-1\}\bigr)\;\subseteq\; A\times\mathbf{S}^0.$$

Both pieces are closed in $A\times\mathbf{S}^0$, so their union $B$ is closed.

### No continuous selection exists

Any $f\in F$ must satisfy $f(a)\in B_a$ for every $a$. In particular

$$f(a)=+1 \text{ for all } a\in[0,\tfrac12), \qquad f(a)=-1 \text{ for all } a\in(\tfrac12,1].$$

Suppose $f$ were continuous. The domain $A=[0,1]$ is connected, while the codomain $\mathbf{S}^0=\{-1,+1\}$ carries the discrete topology. A continuous map from a connected space into a discrete space is constant. Yet the constraints above force

$$f(0)=+1 \neq -1 = f(1),$$

a contradiction. Hence no continuous function lies in $F$.

### Conclusion

The closedness of $A$, the closedness of each fiber $B_a\subseteq\mathbf{S}^{n-1}$, and the closedness of the bundle $B\subseteq A\times\mathbf{S}^{n-1}$ do **not** guarantee the existence of a continuous selection $f:A\to\mathbf{S}^{n-1}$ with $f(a)\in B_a$. The answer to the question is **no**.

### PROOF COMPLETE
